headline: Tesla plans to stop making its Cybertruck

sources.title: Tesla to wind down Cybertruck production as Elon Musk focuses on robotics and AI (The Guardian)
Tesla to wind down Cybertruck production in Texas next year to ramp Cybercab, Musk says (CNBC)
Musk says Tesla will end Cybertruck production in 2027 (CBS News)
Tesla to wind down Cybertruck production at Texas factory next year to make room for Cybercab (Fox Business)

chunks.text: Tesla will stop making its Cybertruck, an electric [[pickup truck]] with a sharp, [[boxy]] steel body. Elon Musk, the company's [[chief executive]], shared the news on X, his [[social media site]], on November 6, 2026. Tesla will {{phase out}} the truck at its factory in Austin, Texas, around the middle of 2027. Musk said Tesla needs the factory space to {{ramp up}} [[production]] of the Cybercab, its [[self-driving]] taxi. No other Tesla factory makes the truck.

verbs.correct: To stop making something step by step
verbs.wrong: To sell something at a lower price
verbs.why: Many cities phase out old buses and buy electric ones. Some stores phase out paper bags over a few years. Tesla will phase out the truck at its huge factory in Austin, Texas, around the middle of 2027.

verbs.wrong: To test a new car on a track
verbs.why: Toy companies ramp up work every fall. Farms ramp up hiring when the fruit is ready. Musk said Tesla needs the factory space to ramp up production of the Cybercab, its self-driving taxi.

chunks.text: Musk first {{showed the truck off}} in 2019. Its [[futuristic]] look made it {{stand out}}. Its [[stainless-steel]] body was hard to build. This problem {{held up}} the [[launch]] for years. Tesla {{handed over}} the first trucks to buyers in late 2023. The company said the [[starting price]] would be 60,990 dollars. The truck never went on sale in Europe, because it did not meet [[safety standards]] there.

verbs.correct: To show something proudly to people
verbs.wrong: To sell something for the first time
verbs.why: Car makers show off their new models at big auto shows. My neighbor shows off his garden to every visitor. Musk first showed the truck off in 2019.

verbs.correct: To be easy to see and notice
verbs.wrong: To be hard to drive and park
verbs.why: Red cars stand out in a parking lot. Her bright yellow coat stands out in the crowd. The truck's futuristic look made it stand out.
Snow often holds up flights in the winter. Missing parts hold up repairs at the shop. Problems with its stainless-steel body held up the truck's launch for years.
The seller hands over the keys after you pay. Students hand over their phones before the test. Tesla handed over the first trucks to buyers in late 2023.

chunks.text: Sales of the Cybertruck never {{took off}}. Musk once said [[annual sales]] could reach 250,000 trucks. Its sales {{fell short of}} that goal by a lot. Car industry researchers [[estimate]] that Tesla sold 20,237 Cybertrucks in the U.S. in 2025. Sales {{dropped off}} by 48 percent from the year before. Tesla's Model 3 and Model Y cars {{make up}} most of its sales. A Wall Street [[analyst]], who advises investors, said high prices and weak [[demand]] made the truck's end easy to predict.

verbs.wrong: To be counted by the government
verbs.why: Some songs take off after one viral video. A new app sometimes takes off in just a few weeks. Sales of the Cybertruck never took off.

verbs.correct: To not reach a goal or amount
verbs.wrong: To change a goal or amount
verbs.why: Most new stores fall short of their sales goals in the first year. His test score falls short of what the college asks for. Its sales fell short of Musk's goal of 250,000 a year by a lot.

verbs.wrong: To be checked again by experts
verbs.why: Visitors to the beach drop off after the summer. Orders usually drop off when prices rise. Cybertruck sales dropped off by 48 percent in 2025.

verbs.correct: To form or be part of something
verbs.why: Women make up half of the class. Small businesses make up most of the shops on our street. Tesla's Model 3 and Model Y cars make up most of its sales.

chunks.text: Tesla is now {{moving on}} to robots and artificial intelligence. The Cybercab has two seats and no [[steering wheel]] or pedals. It began giving [[paid rides]] in parts of Austin in September 2026. Tesla wants to {{roll out}} the service to more places, but U.S. safety officials are reviewing the car. The Texas factory will also build Optimus, Tesla's [[humanoid robot]]. Musk said the trucks people already own will {{stick around}} for a long time.

verbs.wrong: To sell part of a company
verbs.why: After college, many students move on to full-time jobs. Our class moves on to a new chapter every week. Tesla is now moving on to robots and artificial intelligence.

verbs.correct: To start offering a new service
verbs.wrong: To test a service in secret
verbs.why: Phone companies roll out new plans every year. Our city rolls out a bike-sharing program each spring. Tesla wants to roll out the Cybercab service to more places.

verbs.wrong: To be made in a new color
verbs.why: Good teachers often stick around at one school for years. Some guests stick around after the party to help clean. Musk said the Cybertrucks people already own will stick around for a long time.

mainIdea.s: Tesla will end Cybertruck production in Texas in 2027 so its factory can build more self-driving taxis. The steel pickup sold far fewer trucks than the company's boss once predicted.
mainIdea.why: Tesla will phase out the truck in mid-2027 to ramp up Cybercab production. Sales fell far short of the 250,000 a year that the boss predicted.

mainIdea.s: Tesla is moving its famous steel truck to a new plant so its Austin factory can focus on robots. Demand stays strong, and buyers want it as much as they did at its 2023 launch.
mainIdea.why: Close, but nobody said the truck will be built somewhere else. Sales dropped off sharply, and demand for the truck was weak.

mainIdea.s: Tesla has opened a large new factory in Europe to build a cheaper electric pickup. The carmaker hopes the first models will reach drivers there before the end of the decade.
mainIdea.why: Tesla will phase out the Cybertruck in Texas, and the truck never went on sale in Europe. The Texas factory will build more Cybercabs instead.

tf.s: Tesla plans to phase out the Cybertruck at its factory in Texas.
tf.why: Tesla will phase out the truck at its factory in Austin, Texas, around the middle of 2027.

tf.s: Musk said Tesla needs the space to build more pickup trucks.
tf.why: He said Tesla needs the space to ramp up production of the Cybercab, its self-driving taxi.

tf.s: Problems with the truck's steel body held up its launch for years.
tf.why: The stainless-steel body was very hard to build, and those problems held up the launch.

tf.s: Sales of the Cybertruck took off and beat Musk's early prediction.
tf.why: Sales never took off. They fell far short of the 250,000 trucks a year that Musk once said were possible.

tf.s: The Cybertruck makes up most of Tesla's sales.
tf.why: Tesla's Model 3 and Model Y make up most of its sales, not the Cybertruck.

tf.s: Tesla is moving on to robots and artificial intelligence.
tf.why: Tesla is moving on to robots and AI, and the Texas factory will also build a humanoid robot.

lines.text: Did you hear that Tesla is going to stop making the Cybertruck?
Really? The steel truck that looks like a big box?
That's the one. Musk says they'll {{phase it out}} in Texas around the middle of 2027.
Why? It sure {{stands out}} on the road.
[[Love it or hate it]], people notice it. But sales never really {{took off}}.
Musk once said they could sell 250,000 trucks a year. In 2025, Tesla sold about 20,000 in the U.S.
Wow. That {{fell short of}} his goal by a lot.
Right. And it cost [[a pretty penny]], too. The cheapest one was supposed to cost almost 61,000 dollars.
A Wall Street analyst said the end was easy to predict.
So what will the factory make instead?
They want to {{ramp up}} production of the Cybercab, Tesla's self-driving taxi.
The one with no steering wheel?
Yes. Tesla wants to {{roll out}} the service to more places. The company is {{moving on}} to robots and AI.
That's a big bet. [[Go big or go home]], I guess.
Musk says the trucks people already own will {{stick around}} for a long time.
Maybe it was just [[ahead of its time]].

expressions.def: Used to say that something happened just as you expected
ex: The kids ate all the cake. No surprise there.

expressions.def: Used to say that you should try something in a bold way or not try at all
ex: He opened three restaurants at once. Go big or go home, he says.

expressions.def: Too new or modern for people to accept when it first appears
ex: That phone was ahead of its time, so few people bought it.
Her music was ahead of its time.
